title: Comedian Abijit Ganguly Leaves Mumbai After Nine Years, Citing 'Life in Hard Mode'
excerpt: Ganguly has moved to Bengaluru with his family, blaming perpetual construction and seeking greenery and space for his baby — the latest entertainer to base himself outside Mumbai.
body:
• Stand-up comedian Abijit Ganguly has left Mumbai for Bengaluru after nine years, announcing the move in an Instagram post last week.
  • His reasons: perpetual construction, and — with a baby in the family — a wish for greenery, space and, eventually, schools with space.
  • Ganguly arrived in Mumbai from Delhi nine years ago and says he loved the city at first; he dates the change to the years after lockdown.
  • He joins a longer list of entertainers who have based themselves outside Mumbai, from Goa to Bengaluru — though some, like Tanmay Bhat, later returned.

Stand-up comedian Abijit Ganguly has moved out of Mumbai after nine years, settling in Bengaluru with his family and explaining the decision in an Instagram post that has struck a nerve well beyond comedy. Ganguly, who arrived in Mumbai from Delhi nine years ago, said he shifted out last week, according to Mint's report of his post.

"Living in Mumbai constantly felt like life in hard mode. And with a baby in picture wanted to have a little bit of greenery and space around. And eventually schools with space."

— Abijit Ganguly, in his Instagram post

'Perpetual state of construction'

Ganguly's central complaint is not rent or work — it is the city's permanent state of being dug up. "Gradually realised the city will be in a perpetual state of construction since that's how contractors and in turn ministers will make money," he wrote, in the post quoted by Indulge Express. "So, they'll always be that next project, next renovation to make your life tough. And if nothing else, they'll break an existing one completed just a few years ago to make something bigger."

https://x.com/ndtv/status/2114164009830351122

He is careful to say the city changed, not just his tolerance. He used to love Mumbai when he arrived from Delhi, he wrote, but something shifted some years back, especially after lockdown — closing with the joke that Mumbai was good to live in as long as "Dilli se aaya hai kya?" used to be an insult. Fatherhood sharpened the decision: greenery and space around the baby now, schools with space later.

Not the first to leave — and not everyone stays away

Mint placed Ganguly's move in a wider pattern of public figures basing themselves outside the Maximum City, for reasons that include commuting, well-being, a quieter environment and business needs. Comedian Tanmay Bhat's path is the closest parallel and the clearest caution: after the collapse of AIB in late 2018, businessman Kunal Shah advised him to consider Bengaluru, where Bhat spent a considerable period relaunching his career, working on health and building digital and investment interests — and then returned to Mumbai, where he now lives and runs his creative agency Moonshot.

Goa has drawn a different set. Television actress Narayani Shastri moved there with her husband, citing Mumbai commutes that can take two to three hours to reach a set. Nafisa Ali and Pooja Bedi chose Goa's slower pace for personal well-being, and choreographer-director Remo D'Souza shifted his primary base there to escape the constant rush. Singer Lucky Ali chose life on a farm in the Himalayan foothills and in Bengaluru's quiet suburbs, while Juhi Chawla and Jai Mehta built an organic farming retreat in Mandwa, keeping a working relationship with Mumbai while spending time away from its pollution.

The reaction, and the caveat

Responses to Ganguly's post were mixed, and many made the obvious counterpoint: construction is not a Mumbai monopoly. "All cities in this country are in perpetual state of construction. Hello from Hyderabad," one user wrote. Another noted that Bengaluru, too, is under development everywhere. Others backed him — "More power to you… very few of us have the courage to admit it and look for better things."

That is the honest shape of the trend. Leaving Mumbai no longer means leaving the industry — streaming, touring and remote production have loosened the city's hold — but it does not always mean leaving for good, as Bhat's return shows. For Ganguly, the stated test is domestic, not professional: whether Bengaluru gives his child the greenery and space Mumbai, in his telling, no longer could.
